title: 1 Kings 18:17–29
context: Ahab calls Elijah the troubler of Israel, but Elijah answers that Ahab and his father’s house have troubled Israel by forsaking the LORD’s commandments and following the Baals. On Mount Carmel, before the people and the four hundred fifty prophets of Baal, Elijah asks how long they will waver between two sides; the Hebrew idiom pictures limping between two options. The contest is set: the God who answers by fire is God. Baal’s prophets call from morning until past noon, leap about the altar, and cut themselves, while Elijah mocks them, but there is no voice and no answer. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the scene as shared ground about the LORD alone as God and the emptiness of idols.

verses.text: When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, “Is that you, you troubler of Israel?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ahab calling Elijah the troubler of Israel. He blames the messenger rather than facing his own sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Ahab’s accusation as typical of those who resist God’s word. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how sin distorts judgment.

verses.text: He answered, “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, in that you have forsaken the LORD’s commandments and you have followed the Baals.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah answering that Ahab and his father’s house have troubled Israel by forsaking the LORD and following the Baals. The true cause is named.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s reply as a clear statement of covenant unfaithfulness. Both traditions commonly read the verse as calling sin by its name (compare Exodus 20:3).

verses.text: Now therefore send, and gather to me all Israel to Mount Carmel, and four hundred fifty of the prophets of Baal, and four hundred of the prophets of the Asherah, who eat at Jezebel’s table.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah calling for all Israel and the prophets of Baal and Asherah to gather at Mount Carmel. He seeks a public decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summons as setting the stage for God’s public vindication. Readers in both traditions commonly note that the prophets eat at Jezebel’s table, showing royal support for Baal worship.

verses.text: So Ahab sent to all the children of Israel, and gathered the prophets together to Mount Carmel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ahab gathering the people and the prophets to Mount Carmel. The king complies with the prophet’s demand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty in bringing the nation to the place of testing. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a simple step toward the contest.

verses.text: Elijah came near to all the people, and said, “How long will you waver between the two sides? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” The people didn’t say a word.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah asking how long the people will waver between two sides, calling them to follow the LORD if he is God. The call presses for a real decision (compare Joshua 24:15).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call as exposing divided loyalty that cannot stand (compare Matthew 6:24). Readers in both traditions commonly note the people’s silence as a sign of their indecision.

verses.text: Then Elijah said to the people, “I, even I only, am left as a prophet of the LORD; but Baal’s prophets are four hundred fifty men.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah stressing that he alone remains as a prophet of the LORD against four hundred fifty prophets of Baal. The odds seem overwhelming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast as setting up God’s power to work through one servant. Both traditions commonly note that Obadiah had hidden other prophets (18:13), so Elijah may mean that he alone stands publicly as the LORD’s prophet.

verses.text: Let them therefore give us two bulls; and let them choose one bull for themselves, and cut it in pieces, and lay it on the wood, and put no fire under; and I will dress the other bull, and lay it on the wood, and put no fire under it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah proposing a fair test with two bulls and no fire. The terms are clear, simple, and public for all to see.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the test as designed to show the LORD alone as God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a bold challenge to Baal worship.

verses.text: You call on the name of your god, and I will call on the LORD’s name. The God who answers by fire, let him be God.” All the people answered, “What you say is good.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah calling for the God who answers by fire to be acknowledged as God, and the people agreeing. The test is accepted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the proposal as aimed at Baal’s claim to rule the storm and the lightning. Both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up a clear demonstration.

verses.text: Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Choose one bull for yourselves, and dress it first, for you are many; and call on the name of your god, but put no fire under it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah letting the prophets of Baal go first since they are many. He gives them every opportunity to succeed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s generosity as heightening the coming display of the LORD’s power. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a fair contest.

verses.text: They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, “Baal, hear us!” But there was no voice, and nobody answered. They leaped about the altar which was made.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prophets of Baal calling from morning until noon with no answer. Their efforts are sincere but futile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the silence as exposing the emptiness of idols (compare Psalm 115:5). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of misplaced devotion.

verses.text: At noon, Elijah mocked them, and said, “Cry aloud, for he is a god. Either he is deep in thought, or he has gone somewhere, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps and must be awakened.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah mocking the prophets at noon, suggesting that Baal is busy, away, or asleep. The sarcasm exposes the absurdity of idol worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the mockery as a sharp contrast with the LORD who neither slumbers nor sleeps (compare Psalm 121:4). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a pointed rebuke, not a model for ordinary speech.

verses.text: They cried aloud, and cut themselves in their way with knives and lances until the blood gushed out on them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prophets crying aloud and cutting themselves until blood flows. Desperation drives them to self-harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as showing the destructive nature of false worship. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, noting the human cost of idolatry.

verses.text: When midday was past, they prophesied until the time of the evening offering; but there was no voice, no answer, and nobody paid attention.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prophets continuing until the evening offering with no voice, no answer, and no attention. Their god is silent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the threefold silence as a decisive judgment on Baal. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for the LORD’s answer.
